content: Do not discontinue atenolol abruptly without consulting your physician. Stopping atenolol suddenly can lead to chest pain, a heart attack, or an irregular heartbeat. Your physician will likely reduce your dosage gradually to prevent these complications. It is also used to prevent angina (chest pain) and to treat heart attacks. Atenolol belongs to a class of drugs known as beta blockers. It functions by slowing the heart rate and relaxing blood vessels, thereby reducing the workload on the heart. Atenolol is available in tablet form and is taken orally, typically once or twice daily. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take atenolol exactly as prescribed; do not alter the dosage or frequency without medical advice. It may take one to two weeks to experience the full benefits of the medication. Continue taking atenolol even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. Atenolol may also be used for other purposes, such as preventing migraines, managing alcohol withdrawal symptoms, treating heart failure, or addressing irregular heartbeats. Discuss the potential risks and benefits of using atenolol for these conditions with your doctor. If you have questions about other possible uses, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Before starting atenolol, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to atenolol or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Specifically, mention calcium channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem, verapamil), clonidine, NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin), and reserpine, as these may interact with atenolol. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication regimen or monitor you closely for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of asthma, other lung diseases, diabetes, severe allergies, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, heart failure, a slow heart rate, circulation problems, or kidney or heart disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking atenolol, contact your doctor immediately. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your surgeon or dentist that you are taking atenolol. Be aware that atenolol may exacerbate allergic reactions and reduce the effectiveness of injectable epinephrine in treating them. If your doctor recommends a low-salt or low-sodium diet, adhere to these dietary instructions carefully. If you miss a dose of atenolol, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Atenolol may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they persist or worsen: dizziness, lightheadedness, fatigue, drowsiness, depression, upset stomach, or diarrhea. Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience shortness of breath, swelling in the hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, unusual weight gain, or fainting. If you encounter any other unusual symptoms, inform your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store atenolol in its original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly; consult your pharmacist for guidance. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Symptoms of overdose may include extreme fatigue, difficulty breathing, wheezing, slow or rapid heartbeat, fainting, swelling in the extremities, unusual weight gain, shakiness, dizziness, sweating, confusion, blurred vision, headache, numbness or tingling in the mouth, weakness, pale skin, or sudden hunger. Attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor. Your doctor may also ask you to check your pulse; if it is abnormally fast or slow, contact your doctor. Do not share this medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist. Atenolol is sold under the brand names Tenormin® and Tenormin® I.V. Combination products containing atenolol include Tenoretic®, which also contains chlorthalidone.
